title: The Wedding Feast and the Trap Questions
summary: Jesus tells a parable of a king whose invited guests refuse his son's wedding banquet, so the hall is filled with people from the streets, though one guest without wedding clothes is thrown out. Then three groups test him in turn: Pharisees and Herodians on paying taxes to Caesar, Sadducees on the resurrection, and a lawyer on the greatest commandment. Jesus answers each, and then asks his own question about how the Christ can be both David's son and David's Lord, which silences them all.
story: This is still the Tuesday of Jesus' last week, as most readers reconstruct it, in the temple courts. In chapter 21 the chief priests and elders challenged his authority and he answered with parables of judgment. The third of those parables opens this chapter. Then the leaders change tactics: instead of challenging him openly, they try to trap him with questions designed to discredit him before the crowds or put him in danger with Rome. Each attempt fails, and the chapter ends with no one daring to question him further. Having silenced his opponents, Jesus will turn in chapter 23 to denounce the scribes and Pharisees publicly.
historical:
The tax question sat on a live wire. When Judea came under direct Roman rule in AD 6, Rome imposed a census and a head tax, and Judas the Galilean led a revolt against it on the ground that paying tribute to Caesar denied that God alone was Israel's king (Acts 5:37 remembers him). The tax had to be paid in Roman coin. The silver denarius of the emperor Tiberius (ruled AD 14 to 37) carried his portrait and an inscription calling him son of the divine Augustus, which many Jews regarded as offensive. If Jesus said pay, he would lose the crowds who resented Rome; if he said do not pay, the Herodians, supporters of the ruling Herodian family who governed at Rome's pleasure, could report him as a rebel.

The Sadducees were the party of the priestly aristocracy, closely tied to the temple leadership. They rejected the Pharisees' oral traditions and held to the written law, and they denied the resurrection of the dead, as Acts 23:8 also notes. Their question about seven brothers draws on levirate marriage (from the Latin for brother-in-law), the law in Deuteronomy 25:5-10 that a man should marry his dead brother's childless widow to carry on his brother's name. They meant the scenario to make resurrection look absurd.
cultural:
Royal weddings in the ancient world lasted days, and invitations came in two stages: a first invitation, then a summons when the feast was ready. To refuse the second, after accepting the first, was a public insult to the host, and to mistreat the messengers was an act of rebellion against the king. The Jewish hope for the age to come was often pictured as a great banquet (Isaiah 25:6), so Jesus' hearers would have understood that the feast stood for God's kingdom.

Asking which commandment was greatest was a standard question among Jewish teachers, who counted many commandments in the law and debated how they related. Jesus answers with two texts every pious Jew knew. The first is from Deuteronomy 6:5, part of the Shema, the confession of the one God recited morning and evening. The second is from Leviticus 19:18. Joining them was not unknown in Jewish teaching, but Jesus makes them the frame on which the whole law and the prophets hang. His final question uses Psalm 110:1, a psalm attributed to David, and assumes the common belief that the Messiah would be David's descendant.
literary: The chapter has two parts: a parable that completes the trilogy begun in 21:28, and a series of four controversy exchanges. The three test questions come from three different groups and cover politics, doctrine, and the law, and each is introduced with flattery or a clever setup. The pattern builds to a reversal: after being questioned three times, Jesus asks the question, and the chapter closes with total silence (verse 46). Watch too how the parable moves in two stages, like the one before it. First comes the refusal and punishment of the invited guests, then the gathering of new guests, both evil and good, and then a second scene of scrutiny that keeps the parable from becoming a story about cheap entry.

outline.t: The parable of the wedding banquet

doctrines.note: The kingdom is a feast given by a king for his son, and the invitation goes out to the streets once the first guests refuse. Entry is by invitation, not merit, yet the man without wedding clothes shows that the invitation calls for a changed life.

Against the Sadducees Jesus affirms the resurrection of the dead from God's own words at the burning bush: the God of Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob is God of the living. Resurrection life is not a copy of this life's arrangements; it rests on the power of God and his faithfulness to those he has called his own.
Jesus sums up the law in love for God with the whole self and love for neighbor. These do not replace the commandments; they show what all the commandments were for.

By asking how David can call his descendant Lord, Jesus shows that the Messiah is more than a restored Davidic king. Psalm 110 became one of the New Testament's key texts for Jesus' exaltation to God's right hand.

words.note: Eikon, image or likeness, the word for Caesar's portrait on the coin. Jewish hearers knew that humans were made in the image of God (Genesis 1:27). If the coin bearing Caesar's image can be given back to Caesar, the answer implies that what bears God's image, the human person, belongs to God.

Apodidomi, to give back or pay what is owed. Jesus' word in verse 21 frames the tax as returning to Caesar something that is already his, a limited debt, while placing a prior and total claim under God's. It neither baptizes Rome's rule nor calls for revolt.

Eklektos, chosen or elect. In verse 14 the called are the many invited, and the chosen are those who actually take their place at the feast rightly clothed. The saying warns against presuming on an invitation; how it relates to God's electing grace is discussed under the hard question.

Anastasis, resurrection, literally a standing up. It means the raising of the dead to bodily life in the age to come, not the survival of the soul alone. The word appears four times here, and Matthew's Gospel will end with Jesus' own resurrection.

christ: The chapter shows Jesus as the king's son for whom the feast is given, the teacher whose wisdom silences every party, and the Lord of David. The parable places him at the center of God's purposes: the whole banquet is for the son, and refusing the invitation is refusing him. His answer to the Sadducees previews the resurrection he will soon undergo, and his reading of Psalm 110 points beyond it to his exaltation. The early church repeatedly used that psalm to confess that the risen Jesus sits at God's right hand (Acts 2:34-36, Hebrews 1:13). The son of David is also David's Lord, human by descent and exalted above every king.

hard.q: Why is the man without wedding clothes thrown out, when the guests were gathered off the streets with no warning?
hard.a: The scene looks unfair at first: people were brought in from the crossroads, both evil and good, and then one is judged for his clothing. Some interpreters have suggested that hosts supplied garments for guests, which would make his lack a refusal; there is no firm ancient evidence for such a custom, so that reading should be held loosely. The man's silence when asked suggests he had no excuse. Most readers take the garment as a picture of the response the invitation calls for. Many Protestant interpreters see it as the righteousness God gives, echoing Isaiah 61:10's garments of salvation. Many others, noting Matthew's steady stress on doing the Father's will and bearing fruit, see it as the changed life of repentance and obedience. The two readings can be held together: grace invites everyone, and grace does not leave a guest unchanged. Verse 14 then warns that being among the called does not guarantee being among the chosen, a saying that has been read both in terms of God's election and in terms of the human response.

questions: The first guests refused because they were busy with fields and business, not because they hated the king. What ordinary things crowd out God's invitation for you?
What belongs to Caesar in your life, and what belongs only to God? Where do those claims pull against each other?
Jesus hangs the whole law on love for God and neighbor. Which of the two do you find easier to practice, and what does that reveal?
